_readme: State profile for tools/generate_location_pages.py; schema is documented in data/location-state-profiles/IN.json.
name: Missouri

northwest.label: Northwest Prairie
climate: {county} County is in the Northwest Prairie, which is division 1 of NOAA's six Missouri climate divisions. The Missouri Climate Center says that Missouri "has a continental type of climate marked by strong seasonality" and that "The basic gradient for most climatic characteristics is along a line diagonally crossing the state from northwest to southeast." It puts mean annual precipitation at "a low of 34 inches in the northwest to a high of 50 inches in the southeast," and says that in northwestern Missouri "June precipitation, for example, averages five times greater than January precipitation."

NOAA's state climate summary for Missouri gives annual average precipitation as ranging from "a low of 35 inches in the northwest to a high of 55 inches in the southeast," and says the northern part of the state "receives more snowfall, with an annual average of more than 20 inches compared to less than 5 inches in the south." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

The Climate Center says tornadoes "have been observed during every month of the year, with about 70 percent occurring during the 4 months, March through June," and that hail "also occurs in all regions" and that "May has the greatest number of days with hail." NOAA's summary says "Severe thunderstorms are common in Missouri" and describes an April 10, 2001 storm that produced hail "as large as 3 inches in diameter" and "catastrophic hail damage across the I-70 corridor." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

northeast.label: Northeast Prairie
climate: {county} County is in the Northeast Prairie, which is division 2 of NOAA's six Missouri climate divisions. The Missouri Climate Center says that "mean July precipitation is greatest in northeastern Missouri, largely the result of high-intensity convectional precipitation (4.4 inches), and least in southwestern Missouri (3.2 inches)." It also says that "The metropolitan areas of St. Louis and Kansas City exert a significant and measurable effect on their climates," with temperatures "elevated in both regions by a few degrees."

NOAA's state summary says Missouri's "location in the interior of North America and the lack of mountain barriers to the north and south expose the state to incursions of cold arctic air masses in the winter and warm, moist air masses from the Gulf of Mexico in the summer." The Climate Center says the northern half of the state averages about 110 winter days with temperatures below freezing. It says snow has been known to fall as early as October and as late as May, and that "most of it falls in December, January, and February." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

The Climate Center lists "high-intensity rains, protracted drought, heat waves and cold waves, ice storms, windstorms, and tornadoes" among Missouri's extreme climatic events and says that "All of Missouri experiences 'extreme' climate events, and such events must be considered part of the normal climate." NOAA's summary adds that "Missouri has experienced an increase in the number of extreme precipitation events," and that for large portions of the state "more than 40% of the total annual precipitation occurs on the 10 wettest days of the year." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

westcentral.label: West Central Plains
climate: {county} County is in the West Central Plains, which is division 3 of NOAA's six Missouri climate divisions. The Missouri Climate Center says the northern half of the state, the West Central Plains and the East Ozarks average about 110 winter days with temperatures below freezing. It says that "While winters are cold and summers are hot, prolonged periods of very cold or very hot weather are unusual."

The Climate Center says that in summer, temperatures reach 90 degrees Fahrenheit or higher on an average of 40 to 50 days in the west and north and 55 to 60 days in the southeast. It puts mean annual precipitation at "a low of 34 inches in the northwest to a high of 50 inches in the southeast." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

The Climate Center says that "Thunderstorms have been observed in Missouri during the winter months, but they are most frequent from April to July," and that "Measurable precipitation occurs on an average of about 100 days a year." NOAA's state summary says "Missouri has a long and deadly history of tornadic storms" and records that on May 22, 2011 an EF5 tornado hit Joplin. These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

westozarks.label: West Ozarks
climate: {county} County is in the West Ozarks, which is division 4 of NOAA's six Missouri climate divisions. The Missouri Climate Center says "The Ozark region gets abundant rainfall in an average year, and has numerous streams and many springs," and that about 100 winter days fall below freezing in the West Ozarks. It says that "Once every two years in southwestern Missouri one should expect one precipitation event to produce at least 4.5 inches of rain in a 24-hour period."

NWS Springfield's severe weather climatology says "From 1961 to 1995, 367 tornadoes were reported in the NWSO Springfield CWA with an average of 10.5 occurring each year." The same paper says "April and May are the two most active hail months in the Springfield CWA" and "June is the most active month with April a close second" for damaging wind. These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

The Climate Center says mean July precipitation is "least in southwestern Missouri (3.2 inches)." NOAA's Missouri summary says "Severe thunderstorms are common in Missouri" and that severe drought is "a natural part of Missouri's climate." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

eastozarks.label: East Ozarks
climate: {county} County is in the East Ozarks, which is division 5 of NOAA's six Missouri climate divisions. The Missouri Climate Center says "The Ozark region gets abundant rainfall in an average year, and has numerous streams and many springs." It says about 110 winter days fall below freezing in the East Ozarks, "the northern half, the West Central Plains, and East Ozarks" sharing that figure.

The Climate Center says that "Tributary flooding resulting from heavy rains and which may be expected once or twice in most years, and flash flooding along minor streams following heavy thunderstorm rains, occur most frequently in the spring and early summer, April to July, but may occur during any month." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

NOAA's Missouri summary says "Annual average precipitation varies widely across the state" and records that in 2012 a severe drought across the Midwest had large impacts on Missouri. These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

bootheel.label: Bootheel
climate: {county} County is in the Bootheel, which is division 6 of NOAA's six Missouri climate divisions. The Missouri Climate Center says the Bootheel counties average about 70 winter days with temperatures below freezing, against about 110 days in the northern half of the state. It says that "In contrast, in southeastern Missouri, seasonality in precipitation is insignificant due to the greater influence of subtropical air masses throughout the year."

The Climate Center says that in the southeast the average dates of the last spring and first fall moderate freeze are March 16 and November 20. It puts mean January minimum temperature at 12 degrees Fahrenheit in the northwest and 24 degrees in the southeast. These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

NOAA's Missouri summary puts the high end of annual average precipitation at 55 inches in the southeast and says the "winter warming trend is reflected in a below average number of very cold nights since 1990." These are statewide or regional figures, not measurements taken in {county} County.

St. Louis.roofing:
For January 2016 through December 2025, the NOAA Storm Events Database holds 163 hail reports for St. Louis County on 44 separate days. Counted by month, May has 64 of the reports, March 52 and April 20; the other 27 are spread from February through December, and June is the largest of those with 13. Two dates carry 77 of the 163: March 14, 2025 with 43 reports and May 16, 2025 with 34. A stone diameter of 2.00 inches or larger is given on 15 of the reports, and the largest figure in the file, 2.50 inches, includes an entry filed under Allenton on May 26, 2024.

NOAA's narrative for April 1, 2024 puts the largest stones at 1.75 to 2 inches, "reported in Chesterfield and later in Ferguson," and lists severe hail in Wildwood, Maryland Heights, Woodson Terrace, Bridgeton, Hazelwood, Florissant, Dellwood and Jennings. The March 14, 2024 narrative describes another wide swath of hail up to two inches in diameter that fell in Fenton, Valley Park, Sunset Hills, Crestwood, Sappington, Webster Groves, Shrewsbury and Lakewood. On July 9, 2021 the narrative has hail up to two inches in diameter across Bridgeton, St. Ann, Overland, Maryland Heights, Creve Coeur and Brentwood.

Some wind entries describe roofs directly. The April 15, 2023 entry filed under Morschels carries a magnitude of 87 knots, which NOAA marks as estimated, and its narrative says thunderstorm winds "took most of the roof off of an outbuilding" and were estimated between 74 and 100 mph. A March 14, 2025 entry filed under South Bellefontaine says winds "tore the roof off a garage and off a portion of the connected home." NOAA lists 17 tornado reports on 10 days for the county in these files, and the earliest is dated December 10, 2021. The April 1, 2024 South Bellefontaine entry is an EF0 whose narrative reports "minor damage to the roofs of multiple residences," and the April 15, 2023 Morschels entry is an EF1 with "minor roof damage to a couple of houses." The March 14, 2025 entry filed under Clarkson Valley is rated EF2 and gives a path of 20.67 miles with a maximum width of 880 yards; its narrative says the tornado "reached peak surveyed intensity just south of St. Louis Lambert International Airport, where a house sustained EF-2 damage (122 mph)."

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25034 and B25035) counts 446,192 housing units in St. Louis County and puts the median year built at 1969. The largest decade band is the 1960s with 82,127 units (18.4 percent), followed by the 1950s with 81,063 and the 1970s with 71,197. Another 28,196 units date from the 1940s and 43,354 from 1939 or earlier, so the bands through 1979 add up to 305,937 units, or 68.6 percent of the total. The age of a house is only a starting point, so find out when your roof itself was last replaced.

St. Louis County and the City of St. Louis are separate jurisdictions. The Census Bureau's county code file lists them as two entries with different codes, 29189 for the county and 29510 for the city, and every number on this page is for the county only. Permit practice can differ from one municipality to the next, as the two pages below show, so they are examples and not a rule for every street. The City of Kirkwood's building remodeling page says "Permits are issued and inspections are required for all new construction, and the remodeling and repair of existing structures in the City of Kirkwood to insure compliance with the appropriate codes," and lists 314-822-5823 with hours of Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. The City of Florissant's permits page lists the work it requires permits for as "fences, swimming pools, decks and porches, sheds, room additions, basement remodeling, garages, fireplaces, patio covers, electrical wiring, plumbing work, water heater replacement, and furnace and air conditioner installation"; roofing is not named in that list, and the page gives Public Works at 314-839-7648 for questions. Because neither page settles whether a re-roof needs a permit, ask the department that covers your address before work begins.

Other wind entries in the file put roof material and shingles in their narratives. The June 14, 2017 entry filed under Breckenridge Hills says "Roofing material was blown off of the buildings at Northwest Plaza onto the parking lot." On July 14, 2018 an entry filed under Burke City says a tree fell "onto a house on South Hartnett Avenue causing moderate roof damage" between Florissant and Dellwood. On August 12, 2021 an entry filed under Vigus says "In Eureka, several houses had minor shingle damage." On April 18, 2024 an entry filed under Sappington reports that "Some reported shingles blown off of roofs, while one reported their entire roof had blown off." On May 7, 2024, an entry filed under Robinwood West says tree limbs of 6 to 8 inches snapped in Maryland Heights and "A few of these punctured holes in a house roof." On March 14, 2025, one entry filed under Burke City says winds "caused roof damage to multiple homes in the area," and another filed under South Bellefontaine says a mid-sized home had damage to "the entire front side of their roof" and was under a tarp when the report was made. Each of these is a single NOAA entry, and some cover one address while others cover several communities, so none of them tells you what happened to any one roof.

The National Weather Service office in St. Louis also keeps its own review of one earlier storm. Its page on April 22, 2011 describes an EF4 tornado that "tore a path of destruction from west to east across the St. Louis Metropolitan Area, from St. Louis County Missouri eastward across the Mississippi River into Madison County Illinois." That page is NWS's county tornado listing, which says "Data available through 1/1/2013."

The entry dated March 14, 2025, filed under Vigus, reads: "Thunderstorm winds blew an entire intact garage or shed roof onto the ground and into a standing tree, splitting the roof around the tree."

Treat the roof section of any written bid as a short list of decisions rather than one price. The first decision is whether the old shingles are stripped to bare boards or whether a new layer is laid over them. Stripping lets whoever does the work see the wood deck; an overlay does not. Neither choice is wrong by definition, but the bid should say which one is meant, and it should say what happens if soft or stained boards turn up once the old surface is gone.

Next, read down the flashing items. Brick chimneys, plumbing stacks, wall-to-roof joints and the points where two slopes meet are places where water can get in, so a bid that mentions only shingles and a total leaves out the parts a homeowner most wants spelled out. Look for words such as step flashing, counter flashing, drip edge, ridge cap and pipe boots, and look for a note on whether the old metal is reused or replaced.

Then compare how each bid treats the lowest edge of the roof and the valleys. Some bids add a self-sealing membrane there, and some do not. If one bid names it and another is silent, the two totals are not measuring the same job. Do the same with underlayment, starter strips and attic airflow: intake at the eaves, exhaust near the ridge, and whether anything is blocking the soffit.

Keep photographs of the roof from the ground and, if you can do it safely, of any ceiling stains inside, dated before work starts. Ask for the shingle maker and product line by name, the color, the number of bundles, and the warranty paper that comes with them. Ask who will be on the property, what is to be done with old nails and torn-off material, and how the yard and gutters will be protected. Finally, keep every page of whatever you sign.
St. Louis.siding:
NOAA's Storm Events Database lists 125 thunderstorm wind reports for St. Louis County on 65 days between January 2016 and December 2025. July leads by report count with 23 entries on 15 days, followed by May with 22 on 12, June with 21 on 13, March with 18 on only 2 days, August with 18 on 12 and April with 17 on 7. March looks heavy only because of March 14, 2025, which alone carries 16 of the 125 reports; the next busiest dates are April 15, 2023 with 6 and April 26, 2016, May 19, 2022 and May 16, 2025 with 4 each. All 125 entries carry a magnitude; 28 of them are 65 knots or higher, and the highest four are 87, 80, 78 and 78 knots.

Several entries name siding or trim in their own words. A March 14, 2025 entry filed under Oakville says thunderstorm winds "peeled a large amount of siding from a home and caused damage to the roof trim" at an estimated 75 knots. The May 26, 2024 hail narrative, which names cities from Eureka and Wildwood to Webster Groves and Lemay, adds "There were reports of wind driven hail causing damage to the siding of homes." The same afternoon, a supercell wind entry filed under Hollow describes "a central air conditioning unit blown over, a metal backyard canopy lofted into another yard, and significant damage to shingles" across southern St. Louis County. Two tornado entries are just as specific. On March 14, 2024 an EF0 filed under Hanley Hills "caused minor shingle, soffit and gutter damage to two houses," and "Another home sustained moderate siding damage." On May 26, 2024 an EF1 filed under Mattese "caused minor damage to roofs and siding on a couple of houses," and one house lost the roof over its carport.

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25024 and B25003) shows what the housing in St. Louis County is made of. Of 446,192 housing units, 321,187 (72.0 percent) are detached single-family houses and 20,308 are attached single-family units. Buildings with 5 to 19 units hold 45,908 units, buildings with 20 or more hold 28,157, and 1,546 are mobile homes. Of 413,849 occupied units, 286,530 (69.2 percent) are lived in by their owners and 127,319 by renters, which matters because the person who decides on exterior work is not always the person who lives there. By year built, the survey counts 53,584 units from the 1980s, 39,817 from the 1990s, 27,989 from the 2000s, 15,700 from the 2010s and 3,165 from 2020 or later. A repair estimate is easier to compare when it states the material and the wall area it covers.

More wind entries describe what a falling limb or a gust did to a house. On June 19, 2021, an entry filed under Spirit of St. Louis Airport says a 77 mph gust was recorded at the airport at 5:28 p.m. and that trees were down across western parts of the county in Chesterfield, Wildwood, Ellisville, Clarkson Valley and Ballwin. On July 14, 2023 an entry filed under Burke City says part of a large tree fell onto a house in Spanish Lake, "damaging the chimney and roof." On March 14, 2025 an entry filed under Grover says branches fell "on a second story deck causing it to collapse" and that a tree on the roof made a brick chimney crumble. The August 17, 2025 entry filed under Lambert Field says the airport's weather station measured a 58 mph gust from microburst winds and that shortly after, "a large oak tree fell onto a home causing significant damage."

The Missouri Climate Center's page on the state's climate gives context for these gusts. It lists "windstorms" among the extreme climatic events that "must be considered part of the normal climate," and says that these events, "Though infrequent in occurrence and often very geographically restricted," can lead to other environmental disturbances. The same page says that "Tornadoes have been observed during every month of the year, with about 70 percent occurring during the 4 months, March through June," and that "About 82 percent of the Missouri tornadoes occur between noon and midnight."

The paperwork you collect for a siding project should describe your own house. Start by deciding what you are asking for: repair of a few damaged boards, replacement of one wall, or the whole house. A bid for a single elevation is a different product from a bid for four, and a partial job raises the question of how new boards will look beside weathered ones.

Ask whoever prepares each bid to name the product, not just the category. Vinyl, fiber cement, engineered wood and aluminum each come with their own profile widths, color ranges and fastening rules, and the bid should give the manufacturer, the line, the color and the thickness or gauge. Ask whether the color is baked into the board or painted on, and whether touch-up material is left with you.

What goes under the siding deserves its own line. Look for house wrap or another water-resistive layer, flashing above windows and doors, and a plan for the corners and the bottom edge where the wall meets the foundation. If any old boards are removed, ask what will be done if rot or insects are found behind them, and whether a price for that extra work is stated in advance instead of being worked out on the day.

Walk the house with a notepad before the first visit. Note the downspouts, light fixtures, outlets, dryer vents and hose bibs that sit on the wall, since each one has to be taken off and put back or cut around. Photograph the existing siding in daylight, wall by wall. Compare bids line by line, keep the written copies.
St. Louis.windows:
Every NOAA hail entry carries a stone size, so start there. Of the 163 hail reports for St. Louis County from 2016 through 2025, 42 give a diameter of 1.75 inches or larger and 150 give 1.00 inch or larger. On July 17, 2023 a 2.00 inch report was filed under Cross Keys, and the narrative places hail up to two inches in the Florissant, Black Jack and Spanish Lake areas. The April 1, 2024 narrative lists severe hail from Chesterfield and Wildwood to Ferguson and Jennings and says "Extensive, widespread damage to cars was reported with this event." On May 26, 2024 the narrative says the largest stones, 2 to 2.5 inches, fell in Peerless Park, Crestwood and Webster Groves.

Wind and tornado entries are where glass shows up in NOAA's wording for this county. On April 15, 2023 an entry filed under Ballwin says thunderstorm winds "blew a large section of windows down" at The Pointe, the Ballwin Parks and Recreation center, and that glass blew over into the pool. The May 16, 2025 EF2 entry filed under Clayton says that in Richmond Heights "the tornado blew out the windows of St. Mary's Hospital" and damaged the building's exterior. Those are large buildings, not houses, but the entries show that glass is part of the record and not only roofs and trees.

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25034 and B25035) is a public guide to how old the county's windows could be, since it counts when each building was built and not when its windows were replaced. Of 446,192 housing units, 43,354 were built in 1939 or earlier, 28,196 in the 1940s, 81,063 in the 1950s, 82,127 in the 1960s and 71,197 in the 1970s. Another 93,401 date from the 1980s and 1990s, 27,989 from the 2000s, 15,700 from the 2010s and 3,165 from 2020 or later, and the survey puts the median year built at 1969. The same survey counts 286,530 owner-occupied and 127,319 renter-occupied units among 413,849 occupied homes. A window written on a bid can be a replacement of a whole unit or only the sash and glass, so ask whoever writes the bid to say which it is, and to name the frame material, the glass package and any trim work.

The hail file also has a few entries that are not about size at all. The March 14, 2025 date holds the most reports in the file, and one filed under Lemay has an individual reporting "quarter sized hail that was 2 to 3 inches deep on the ground." The June 30, 2023 narrative filed under Saint John describes a wide swath of large hail in northern parts of the county, in Woodson Terrace, Saint John, Bel-Ridge, Kinloch, Ferguson and Cool Valley. On May 19, 2025, the Missouri State Highway Patrol reported golf ball sized hail in Florissant, and a photo of a 2 inch hailstone was submitted from Brentwood. An official from the City of Chesterfield submitted a photo of 2 inch hail on May 16, 2025. By year, the hail file holds 93 reports for 2025, 15 for 2016, 14 for 2023 and 11 for 2024, and the other six years together hold 30. Report counts depend on who was watching and reporting, so a high year does not by itself mean more hail fell.

Replacing windows in St. Louis County starts with a decision about method. A full-frame replacement removes the old frame and trim and sets a new unit into the bare opening; an insert, sometimes called a pocket replacement, leaves the existing frame in place and fits a new sash assembly inside it. The first gives access to the framing and flashing around the opening, the second keeps more of the interior trim. A bid should say which approach it uses for every opening.

Measure and count before anyone visits. List each window by room, note how it opens (double-hung, casement, slider, fixed), and mark any that are oversized, arched, or sit above stairs. Photograph each one inside and out. Ask whoever wrote the bid to write the same list back to you with the size, the style and the frame material, so there is no confusion about which line refers to which opening.

Glass specifications are written in a shorthand worth asking about: double or triple panes, a low-emissivity coating, gas fill between the panes, and the spacer along the edge. Ask for the manufacturer's name and series, the stated energy ratings that appear on the product label, and the written warranty for the frame, the glass and the hardware. Ask whether screens, grids and locks are included and what color the interior and exterior will be.

Then ask about the finish work: interior casing, caulk, exterior trim wrap, foam around the frame, and the clean-up of old glass and debris. Ask how furniture and floors inside will be protected. Keep every page of what you sign.

Jackson.roofing:
For January 2016 through December 2025, the NOAA Storm Events Database holds 130 hail reports for Jackson County on 35 separate days. March and May are tied at 32 reports each, April has 15, June, July and August have 12 each, and the rest of the year holds 15. May 26, 2016 is the busiest date with 20 reports, ahead of March 6, 2017 with 12 and March 12, 2024 with 11. 28 reports give a stone diameter of 1.75 inches or larger, and the three largest are 3.00 inches at Sibley and 2.75 inches at Sibley and at Lone Jack Berry Airport. The Sibley entry's narrative reads "Three inch hail was reported at the Jackson County Sheriffs Office."

The episode narrative for March 12, 2024 describes a supercell that developed over the Lee's Summit and Greenwood area, "dropping golf ball or larger hail across portions of Greenwood, Lone Jack, and up toward Oak Grove." It adds that 21 severe thunderstorm warnings were issued and that there were 27 local storm reports of severe hail; the narrative covers the whole episode, and 11 of NOAA's hail entries that date are in Jackson County. The episode narrative for July 19, 2018 describes a line of supercells over the eastern Kansas City metro that "produced significant hail up to baseball size." A hail entry filed under Raytown on April 17, 2019 reads "Quarter to golf ball sized hail fell just south of Kauffman Stadium."

Tornado entries in the county tell their own story about roofs and houses. NOAA lists 15 tornado reports on 9 days between March 2017 and June 2025. The March 6, 2017 EF3 filed under Tarsney Lakes went through Oak Grove, and its narrative says "well built permanent foundation houses completely removed from the foundation and toppled over." The May 2, 2018 EF0 entry filed under Dodson describes large trees that "fell onto houses, causing roof and structural damage," and the Raytown entry for that date reports the same kind of damage. The May 6, 2024 EF1 filed under Blue Springs is described as a "5.5 mile long" tornado that began in south Blue Springs, where in the narrative's words it "destroyed a small gazebo in a residential area," and then reached Grain Valley, damaging commercial buildings along SW Eagles Parkway. On June 3, 2025 two tornadoes were filed, an EF0 near the Truman Sports Complex and an EF1 in Independence whose narrative says "Essentially all of the damage was uprooted trees and large tree branches snapped."

Some wind entries mention roofs outright. The March 6, 2017 entry filed under Leeds sums up downtown Kansas City: "Several images of large structures with major damage to roofs and facades were seen on local news from across the metro." The June 21, 2019 entry filed under Richards-Gebaur says "Roofing material blew off some buildings in the area." Two March 14, 2025 entries are short: "Roof damage to house in Grain Valley" and "Social media report of roof damage to a house from outflow wind gusts" near Lone Jack.

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25034 and B25035) counts 336,288 housing units in Jackson County and puts the median year built at 1970. The largest single-decade band is the 1970s with 48,403 units (14.4 percent), followed by the 1960s with 44,476, the 1950s with 43,394 and the 1980s with 32,395; the open-ended band for 1939 or earlier is larger than any of them at 62,322 (18.5 percent). The bands through 1979 add up to 215,583 units, or 64.1 percent of the county's housing. The age of a house tells you little until you know when the roof itself was last replaced.

Jackson County's own Public Works office handles only part of the county. Its Zoning and Subdivision Applications page says "Jackson County is only responsible for the unincorporated areas of the County. If you have a need within city limits, you should contact the appropriate city." Its Construction Permits page says permits are taken Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. until 3:30 p.m. at the Public Works Tech Center, 303 W. Walnut in Independence, and gives 816-881-4649 for questions. The January 2025 building permit packet for unincorporated Jackson County names the 2018 International Residential Code. Two cities inside the county do publish re-roofing rules. The City of Independence's asphalt shingle guideline says "Building permits are required for re-roofing existing dwellings" and gives the building inspections department at 816-325-7401. The City of Lee's Summit's building permits page says "Permits are required for re-roofing of structures" and lists Development Services at 816.969.1200. For an address inside a city, the county's page says to contact that city, so ask the office that covers your address.

A thunderstorm wind record from March 6, 2017 at Lake Lotawana says, in full: "While surveying the tornado that hit Oak Grove there was a neighborhood just south of the track of the tornadic circulation at Lake Lotawana. This damage was straight line winds, perhaps associated with a real-flank downdraft of the tornadic supercell that produced several tornadoes. The extent of the damage included some shingles off of roofs and some large tree limbs down."

Roof bids are easier to compare once they are lined up on the same items. Begin with scope. Does the bid cover every slope or only the damaged one? Does it include the garage and any porch roof? Does it list the tear-off, the disposal of old shingles and the cleanup with a magnet for stray nails? Write down the answers beside each total.

Pay attention to what lies between the shingles and the wood. Ask for the name of the underlayment, whether a waterproof membrane is placed along the eaves and in the valleys, and how the bid treats the ridge, the hips and the vents. A roof that vents poorly can trap heat and moisture in the attic, so ask whether intake and exhaust openings are being added, cleared, or left as they are.

Ask for the shingle by brand, line, color and style, and for the warranty documents in writing. Architectural and three-tab shingles are not the same product, and the bid should not leave you guessing which is meant. Ask how many nails are used per shingle and where they go, and ask to see the manufacturer's installation sheet. If a bid's author cannot show you the sheet, that is useful to know.

Before work begins, take date-stamped photos of every slope, the gutters and the landscaping beside the house. Ask where the dumpster or trailer will sit and how the lawn will be protected. Make sure the start and end terms are written down.

One more habit pays off with any bid: circle every line that uses a vague word such as allowance, as needed, or if required, and ask what number or condition sits behind it. Vague lines are where two proposals drift apart, and a short list of clarified lines makes the final comparison far simpler. Keep the list beside the photographs you took of the slopes, the ridge and the eaves, so every question points to something you can both see.
Jackson.siding:
For January 2016 through December 2025, NOAA's Storm Events Database lists 275 thunderstorm wind reports for Jackson County on 65 days, more than any other storm type it files for the county. June has 87 of the reports on 16 days and July has 75 on 12, followed by May with 51, August with 20, March with 22 and April with 6. The year counts are uneven: 2025 alone holds 93 reports and 2024 holds 50, against between 8 and 36 in each of the other eight years. The busiest dates are July 11, 2025 with 20 reports, June 3, 2025 with 19, and March 14, 2025 and June 26, 2025 with 16 each. How many reports NOAA files for a date depends on how many people phone in or post them, so these counts show where the file is thick, not necessarily where the wind was strongest.

Only 10 of the 275 entries reach 65 knots, and the highest is 71 knots. The August 12, 2021 entry filed under Fairmont is 71 knots, and its narrative says "A spotter with wind instruments reported a 82 mph wind gust, along with tree and powerline damage." The May 25, 2024 entry filed under Independence is 70 knots, and its narrative says "Measured gust of 80 mph with large oak trees downed just southwest of downtown Independence." Knots and miles per hour are different units, which is why a 70 knot entry can describe an 80 mph gust.

Siding is named in only a few of the county's narratives. The March 6, 2017 entry filed under Grandview says a narrow swath of wind left "several structures had some minor roof and siding damage" and that the damage pattern pointed to straight line thunderstorm wind. A March 14, 2025 entry filed under Oak Grove says siding was torn from a business, and one filed under Fairmont says "Windows blown out at residence in Independence." The July 11, 2025 entry filed under Blue Springs mentions "damage to the roof of a building in Blue Springs" along with downed tree limbs. None of these says what the wall material was, so the entries are weak evidence about any one kind of siding.

Siding follows the shape of the housing, and the 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25024 and B25003) shows that shape for Jackson County. Of 336,288 housing units, 222,780 (66.2 percent) are detached single-family houses, 17,974 are attached, and 23,637 are in buildings of 2 to 4 units. Buildings with 5 to 19 units hold 30,455 units, buildings with 20 to 49 hold 13,985, buildings with 50 or more hold 24,285, and 3,039 units are mobile homes. Of 306,798 occupied units, 181,443 (59.1 percent) are owner-occupied and 125,355 (40.9 percent) are renter-occupied. Year built runs from 62,322 units in 1939 or earlier through 48,403 in the 1970s to 22,032 in the 2010s and 4,580 in 2020 or later. A repair estimate for siding is easier to compare when it names the material, the wall area, and what is done about the trim, flashing and house wrap around the work.

Read a siding bid with the history of your own house in mind. Ask whoever prepares each bid what is on the walls today, whether a layer will be removed or covered, and what is found underneath. If the answer is that it depends, ask for the way any extra repair will be priced before the work begins.

Compare the material choices line by line. Vinyl, fiber cement, wood, engineered wood and metal panels behave differently over decades, need different upkeep, and are installed with different tools. The bid should name the product and the finish, state the profile (lap width or panel size), and say who stands behind the paint or color. Ask for sample pieces and look at them outdoors, in daylight, beside the trim you are keeping.

Ask about the parts that no one sees once the job is finished: the water-resistive barrier, flashing at windows and doors, sealant at joints, and the starter strip at the bottom. Ask what is planned at corners, at gable ends, around vents and under the eaves. A written bid that describes these items is easier to compare than one that lists only a square-foot total.

Walk around the house and mark everything that has to come off and go back: shutters, house numbers, lights, spigots, satellite mounts and electrical boxes. Take photographs of each wall before work starts. Keep the signed bid, any change orders and the product paperwork in one folder.

Finish with a look at the ground. Siding that ends too close to soil or a concrete slab can wick moisture, so ask what clearance is planned along the bottom edge and what is to be done around steps and porch posts. Ask where scrap will be piled each day and whether magnets or sweepers will be used on the driveway before the work area is left.
Jackson.gutters:
Heavy rain is the part of Jackson County's NOAA record most tied to gutters and drainage. For January 2016 through December 2025, the Storm Events Database holds 49 flash flood entries for the county on 15 separate days. Thirty of them are dated 2017, ten are dated 2019, and no other year has more than three; August holds 23 of the 49 and July 13. Four dates carry most of the 2017 entries: August 5 with 11, July 27 and August 22 with 7 each, and August 21 with 4. Many entries are one road or one intersection each, which is why the count is large.

The July 27, 2017 narrative says 5 to 7 inches of rain fell across Kansas City in 3 to 6 hours, with one of the hardest hit areas along Indian Creek near 103rd and Wornall, "due to the record flood for Indian Creek." A separate August 21, 2017 Heavy Rain entry says "A NWS employee recorded 9.2 inches of rain in their rain gauge in Brookside, a subdivision of Kansas City." The August 26, 2016 narrative says "While surrounding areas received up to 11 inches of rain, the KC metro area received 5 to 6 inches over a 2 to 3 hour span." The July 1, 2024 entry says up to 6 inches of rain fell across portions of Jackson County in a couple of hours and caused "widespread flash flooding across much of Jackson County." The August 5, 2017 entries include "Water was 10 inches deep around neighborhoods just SSW of Kansas City" and a road closed at Swope Park because the Blue River put "2 feet of running water over the road."

Not all of the entries are about creeks. The July 4, 2019 entry filed under Lake Lotawana says six to eight inches of water flowed over Langsford Road and Windsboro Road, "not known to have flooded in at least 10 years per the resident." The April 30, 2019 entry filed under Holmes Park says "Storm sewer system was overflowing with some ponding on the roads." And the May 1, 2019 Flood entry filed under Kansas City Downtown says heavy spring rains caused ongoing flooding along the Missouri River through the month, with major flooding at times.

Gutter damage itself rarely appears in these narratives, but wind and tree damage to roof edges does. The May 2, 2018 tornado narrative describes trees falling onto houses in Raytown with roof damage, and the May 19, 2025 Lee's Summit entry says "Downed tree damaged a roof on a property in Lees Summit." The Missouri Climate Center says that "Spring, summer, and early fall precipitation comes largely in the form of showers or thunderstorms," and that the Missouri River "flows eastward across the State from Kansas City." The Climate Center also says "Serious flooding occurs less frequently along the main stems of the Missouri and Mississippi Rivers and usually occurs during the spring and early summer." When you compare repair estimates for gutters, ask how many downspouts the job uses, where each one discharges, and whether the estimate covers fascia boards if they are rotted.

Before collecting any gutter bid in Jackson County, spend ten minutes outside while it rains. Watch where water pours over the edge, where it pools at the foundation, and whether any downspout empties onto a walkway or driveway. Mark those spots on a sketch of the house. The sketch gives everyone who prepares a bid the same starting information and gives you something to hold up against the written proposal.

Ask what the new system is made of and how it is shaped. Aluminum, steel and copper are all offered; half-round and K-style profiles look different and carry water differently. Ask for the width, the material thickness, the finish and how long each run will be. Ask whether the runs are formed in one piece on site or joined from sections, because every joint is a place where leaks can start.

Ask where downspouts will be placed and where they will empty. Extensions, splash blocks and underground pipes all do different things, and a bid should say what is included. Ask about slope along each run, the spacing of the hangers, and what the gutters will be fastened to. If the fascia behind them is damaged, ask how the bid handles that repair.

Ask also about leaf guards, which some people add and others skip. They are an extra, so the line should be separate and the maker named. Keep photographs of the existing gutters, notes from the rain walk and every page of the paperwork.
Jackson.windows:
Every NOAA hail entry carries a stone size, so start there. Of 130 hail reports from 2016 through 2025, 114 give a diameter of 1.00 inch or larger and 6 give 2.00 inches or larger. The 2.00 inch entries include Buckner on May 26, 2016, Fairmont on March 6, 2017 and Lake Lotawana on July 19, 2018, and the larger ones include the 3.00 inch Sibley entry and the 2.75 inch entry at Lone Jack Berry Airport. A March 6, 2017 trained-spotter entry filed under Lake City reports "golf ball sized hail" at the Lake City Ammo Plant. An August 24, 2016 entry filed under Richards-Gebaur reads "Golf ball sized hail at Highway 71 and 150." An October 11, 2023 entry filed under Oak Grove carries a photo of "golf ball sized hail between Grain Valley and Oak Grove."

Few of Jackson County's hail entries carry a narrative at all, so this record says more about size than about damage. A March 12, 2024 entry filed under Lee's Summit places quarter sized hail at Summit Ridge Apartments off Tudor Road. Month by month, the hail entries are 7 in February, 32 in March, 15 in April, 32 in May, 12 in June, 12 in July, 12 in August, 5 in September, 2 in October and 1 in December. Spread over 35 days, that is 7, 4, 6 separate days in March, April and May. The Missouri Climate Center says that "Hail also occurs in all regions and may occur throughout the year, but it is much less likely in winter. May has the greatest number of days with hail."

Wind and tornado entries are where glass appears. A March 14, 2025 entry filed under Fairmont says "Windows blown out at residence in Independence." The EF0 tornado of March 6, 2017 filed under Vale was in Lee's Summit; its narrative reports "a facade failure to a local business" and says "Otherwise the damage was relegated to tree damage in Lee's Summit." The Grandview entry of the same evening speaks of "some minor roof and siding damage" to several structures.

The 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25034 and B25035) shows when Jackson County's 336,288 housing units were built, which is a public clue to how old their windows could be. Units from the 1970s number 48,403, from the 1960s 44,476, from the 1950s 43,394, from the 1940s 16,988 and from 1939 or earlier 62,322. The 1980s hold 32,395, the 1990s 32,111, the 2000s 29,587, the 2010s 22,032 and 2020 or later 4,580, and the median year built is 1970. The survey counts 181,443 owner-occupied and 125,355 renter-occupied homes, so a large share of the county's windows belong to a landlord, not the person who lives behind them. A window quote is easier to compare when it says whether the whole unit or only the sash is replaced, what the frame is made of, and who handles the interior and exterior trim.

Window bids in Jackson County are easier to judge when you do your own survey first. Go room to room and list each opening with its approximate size, how it operates and whether it is original to the house. Mark windows that stick, sweat, rattle or let in air. Take a photograph of each from inside and one from outside. Then give the same list to everyone who prepares a bid, so that every written proposal covers the same openings.

Ask whoever prepares each bid to state the replacement method for each opening: full-frame, which takes out the old frame, or insert, which fits a new unit inside the old one. Ask what the frame is made of, whether vinyl, fiberglass, wood or aluminum clad, and what the glass package includes. Look for the maker's name, the series, the type of coating, any gas fill and the performance figures on the label that comes with each unit.

Ask about flashing, foam and sealant at the edges, since a good window set badly can still leak. Ask who removes the old units, what happens to the glass, and how interior trim is handled. If any window has to be a certain size or shape for an escape route in a bedroom or basement, ask whoever wrote the bid to tell you in writing how that is being handled.

Check what the warranty covers and for how long: frame, glass, seals, hardware, finish, labor. Ask whether it can be passed on if you sell the house. Hold on to the signed contract, the order sheet and every receipt.

Do not forget the small items that surprise people after an install: how the old blinds and curtain rods come down and go back up, whether a screen is included for every opening that had one, and what is done about the paint line where trim was removed. Ask for each of these to be written in the bid, even if the answer is that it is not included.

St. Charles.siding:
For January 2016 through December 2025, NOAA's Storm Events Database lists 81 thunderstorm wind reports for St. Charles County on 55 days. June and July each have 20 reports, on 11 and 13 days, followed by May with 13, August with 10, April with 7, March with 6, February with 2, and one each in September, October and December. Only 5 entries reach 65 knots, and the two highest, 70 knots each, are April 26, 2016 under Cappeln and May 2, 2022 under New Melle. No single date has more than four reports in this county's file, and the busiest are April 26, 2016 with 4 and June 28, 2018, June 5, 2019, June 1, 2019, June 19, 2021 and July 16, 2023 with 3 each.

Several narratives name siding or trim directly. The May 2, 2022 entry filed under New Melle says "In Wentzville, a home sustained minor siding and shingle damage," and that in Lake St. Louis a home "sustained minor shingle damage." The July 15, 2020 entry filed under Gilmore says an 8 inch tree limb fell onto a house in St. Peters "causing minor roof and gutter damage." The August 12, 2023 entry filed under Wentzville Airport says that on the north side of St. Charles a large branch fell onto a house "causing minor roof, soffit and gutter damage," and that in O'Fallon a branch "damaged a vinyl fence." The March 6, 2017 tornado entry filed under Foristell reports "roof and siding damage to a number of homes." The September 26, 2023 hail entry filed under Foristell says "Hailstones damaged windows and siding in multiple neighborhoods in Wentzville." The May 11, 2016 hail narrative says "Reports of windows blown out, roofing and siding damage were common."

Other wind entries are about neighboring parts of a house. On June 19, 2021 an entry filed under St Peters mentions "a garage door was bowed inward on a home in Cottleville." On July 6, 2025 an entry filed under St Peters says winds downed trees at the Sunbrook Apartment Complex and, near Ehlmann Road, blew over light poles and uprooted trees "up to 60 feet in height." On April 26, 2016 an entry filed under Orchard Farm says winds "lifted" a rubber roof membrane on two buildings, "allowing some water into the buildings."

The 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25024 and B25003) describes what St. Charles County's walls are attached to. Of 167,163 housing units, 124,878 (74.7 percent) are detached single-family houses, 12,559 are attached single-family units, and 4,200 are mobile homes. Buildings with 5 to 19 units hold 11,438 units and buildings with 20 or more hold 7,340. Owners live in 129,898 of the 161,311 occupied units (80.5 percent) and renters in 31,413. Year built is weighted toward newer construction: 28,267 units from the 1980s, 32,538 from the 1990s, 35,465 from the 2000s and 24,017 from the 2010s, against 3,646 from 1939 or earlier.

The county's 2021 residential code amendments touch exterior work in one place. In the smoke alarm section, an exception to the rule for alterations that require a permit reads "Work involving the exterior surfaces of dwellings, such as the replacement of roofing or siding, the addition or replacement of windows or doors, or the addition of a porch or deck." Whether your siding job needs a permit is a separate question for the building office that covers your address, and a repair estimate is easier to compare when it states the material, the wall area, and the trim and house wrap work.

Match and finish are what show from the street. Begin by asking whoever prepares each bid to describe the board profile, the exposure (how much of each board shows), the texture, the color and the maker. Ask for a physical sample, and look at it against the brick, stone or trim that stays. Light changes how a color reads, so check in morning and afternoon.

A written bid should address the layer behind the boards. Ask about house wrap or sheathing tape, flashing above openings, and what is placed behind trim and corners. If your house has stone or brick wainscot on the front and siding on the other sides, ask how the siding ends are finished where it meets masonry, and how any gap is sealed.

Ask about the neighborhood rules, too. Some subdivisions have architectural review requirements for exterior changes, and some ask for an approval before work starts. A bid cannot answer that for you, but it can name the product so that you can submit it. Make a list of exterior items attached to the walls and ask how each will be handled.

Ask what protection is placed over shrubs and the lawn, where tools and material are staged, and how scrap is cleared at the end of each day. Keep photographs and the written estimate together.

A last practical point for a house with a covered porch, a bump-out or a walkout lower level: ask for each wall to be listed separately in the paperwork, with its own area figure. A single lump-sum line hides whether the lower wall, the gable peaks or the dormer cheeks are included. When two written proposals differ, check first whether they cover the same walls; that is much easier to spot with a wall-by-wall list.

Keep a short written list of what you were told about lead times for the chosen color, since special colors and trim pieces may be ordered separately from the main boards. Ask what is done if a delivered color does not match the sample you approved, and ask who checks the boxes against the order sheet when material arrives at the house.
St. Charles.windows:
Hail drives the window story for St. Charles County. The NOAA Storm Events Database holds 70 hail reports for the county from 2016 through 2025, and 65 of them give a diameter of 1.00 inch or larger. Fifteen give 2.00 inches or larger, including a run of entries dated May 16, 2025 under Cottleville, Harvester, Weldon, Weldon Spring and Defiance. The Cottleville entry that day is 2.50 inches, and a Weldon entry says "Hail persisted for 10 or more minutes." By year, 2025 holds 36 of the 70 reports, 2016 holds 8, 2024 holds 6 and 2023 and 2019 hold 5 each. Thirty of the 36 reports for 2025 come from one date, May 16. Report counts depend on who was watching and reporting, so a high year does not by itself mean more hail fell.

Two narratives name glass directly. The September 26, 2023 entry filed under Foristell says the thunderstorm "intensified quickly as it entered St. Charles County," with severe hail in and around Wentzville "ranging from quarters to golf balls," and that "Hailstones damaged windows and siding in multiple neighborhoods in Wentzville." The May 11, 2016 narrative says "Reports of windows blown out, roofing and siding damage were common," and that 120 cars at a dealership near I-64 and Highway 94 "sustained busted windows and lots of dents from large hail." The March 27, 2021 entry filed under Weldon says "The National Weather Service reported golf ball sized hail at the office in Weldon Springs." The May 26, 2024 narrative lists "numerous reports of 1 to 2 inch hailstones in eastern St. Charles County impacting St. Peters, St. Charles, and Kampsville."

The county's 2021 residential code amendments have a few lines about windows. Section N1101.5 says construction documents must show details including "Fenestration, U-factors and solar heat gain coefficients (SHGC)." Its replacement Table N1102.1.3 gives a row for climate zone 4A with a fenestration U-factor of .35, and a note saying "U-factors and SHGC are maximums." Its air barrier table says "The space between framing and skylights, and the jambs of windows and doors, shall be sealed." In the smoke alarm section, an exception to the alarm rule for permitted alterations lists "the replacement of roofing or siding, the addition or replacement of windows or doors." Those lines come from an adopted code and say nothing about any one window.

The 2020 to 2024 American Community Survey (5-year tables B25034 and B25035) puts the median year built for St. Charles County's 167,163 housing units at 1994. Units from the 1990s number 32,538, from the 2000s 35,465, from the 2010s 24,017, from the 1980s 28,267 and from the 1970s 19,726. Units from before 1960 total 11,366, and 5,493 were built in 2020 or later. Owner-occupied homes number 129,898, or 80.5 percent of occupied units. When you compare window repair estimates, ask whoever writes the bid to say whether a unit is replaced whole or only the glass or sash, what the frame is made of, and who handles the trim.

Window bids are easier to compare if you keep a clean list. Make a sheet with one row per window: room, width and height as best you can measure, style, whether it is original, and a short note on what is wrong with it. Include the patio door and any basement windows. Hand the sheet to whoever prepares each bid.

Ask for the replacement method in each case: a new frame set into the opening, or a new unit inserted into the old frame. Ask whether the existing trim stays, and if so what is done to protect it. Ask what the frames are made from, whether the glass has a coating and gas fill, and which maker and series are quoted. Ask for the product label details to be added to the paperwork.

Ask about grids, tilt-in sashes, locks, screens and color on each side of the window. Ask who is responsible for removal of old units and for the interior finish: paint, stain, caulk and casing. If your subdivision has rules about exterior appearance, ask whoever wrote the bid to show you the proposed color and grid pattern in writing before you agree.

Collect the written warranty and read what it says about glass seals, frames and hardware. Photograph the windows beforehand.

If any of your windows face the street or sit above a front porch, ask for a note about how ladders and lifts will be placed so the roof, flower beds and walkway are not scuffed. For tall stair windows, ask whether scaffolding is part of the plan and whether it is listed. A proposal that spells these details out is easier to compare with the others in your folder.
